Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## claude.ai PostHog
# PostHog `exec` covers

access-control|action|advanced-activity-logs|agent-feedback|alert|annotation|apm|approval|batch-export|billing|broadcasts|canvas|cdp-function|change|channel|cohorts|comment|conversations|custom-property-sources|dashboard|data|docs-search|domains|early-access-feature|elements-stats|endpoint|error-tracking|event-definition|execute-sql|experiment|explain-chart|external-data|feature-flag|file-download-batch|generate-app-url|health-issues|heatmaps|identity-provider-configs|inbox|insight|integration|llm-total-costs|llma-clustering|llma-dataset|llma-evaluation|llma-offline|llma-parser|llma-personal|llma-prompt|llma-provider|llma-review|llma-score|llma-skill|llma-summarization|llma-trace|logs|marketing-analytics|mcp|media-image|message-categories|metric|notebooks|opt-outs|org-member|organization|path-cleaning-rules|persons|products|project|property-definition|proxy|query|read-data-schema|reminder|reusable-widgets|role|saved-query-column|scheduled-changes|scout|session-recording|signals-scout|skill|sql-variables|subscriptions|survey|switch|tasks-config|usage-metrics|user|view|vision|warehouse|web-analytics|wizard-install|workflows

# Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## claude.ai PostHog
# PostHog `exec` covers

access-control|action|advanced-activity-logs|agent-feedback|alert|annotation|apm|approval|batch-export|billing|broadcasts|canvas|cdp-function|change|channel|cohorts|comment|conversations|custom-property-sources|dashboard|data|docs-search|domains|early-access-feature|elements-stats|endpoint|error-tracking|event-definition|execute-sql|experiment|explain-chart|external-data|feature-flag|file-download-batch|generate-app-url|health-issues|heatmaps|identity-provider-configs|inbox|insight|integration|llm-total-costs|llma-clustering|llma-dataset|llma-evaluation|llma-offline|llma-parser|llma-personal|llma-prompt|llma-provider|llma-review|llma-score|llma-skill|llma-summarization|llma-trace|logs|marketing-analytics|mcp|media-image|message-categories|metric|notebooks|opt-outs|org-member|organization|path-cleaning-rules|persons|products|project|property-definition|proxy|query|read-data-schema|reminder|reusable-widgets|role|saved-query-column|scheduled-changes|scout|session-recording|signals-scout|skill|sql-variables|subscriptions|survey|switch|tasks-config|usage-metrics|user|view|vision|warehouse|web-analytics|wizard-install|workflows

# Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++
</system-reminder>

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part.   entire brain query "<query>" --json       # hybrid (lexical+vector, RRF) — the default
  entire brain query --keyword "<query>" --json      # lexical keyword over memories + history + docs (BM25 for history/docs)
  entire brain query --semantic "<query>" --json     # vector/semantic over memories + docs (+ history/conversation with a Gemma-class embedder)
  entire brain get <id> --json              # fetch one item by id (fact:… | history:… | doc:…)
  entire brain multi-get <id>... --json     # fetch several by id

# Plan: evaluate and improve agent-instruction adherence and memory usefulness

Status: draft, awaiting approval. Not committed (repo policy: no committed docs).

## Goal

Measure how well local coding agents follow the Brain instructions, and how
useful the returned memories are. Then test instruction changes that improve
both, with evidence.

## What "agent instructions" means today (the surfaces under test)

1. `.entire/agent-guide.md` — generated from `internal/agentsetup/guide.go` +
   `strict.go`. Mirrored byte-identical with entire-graph.
2. `internal/agentsetup/brain-reference.md` — the command reference.
3. `templates/entire-brain-recall-*.md` and `entire-brain-intake-*.md` —
   subagent and skill instructions for Claude and Codex.
4. `entire brain brief` output — the memories sample and guidance strings.
5. `entire brain recall` output — the fact record format the agent reads.

## Recorded evidence this plan builds on (Brain citations)

- Permissive guide wording collapsed adherence in real sessions: 332 graph
  calls vs 96,987 exploration calls (0.34%), graph-first rate 0. Directive
  wording is pinned by `TestNormalGuideStaysDirective`
  (comment in `internal/agentsetup/guide.go`).
- A past "agents ignore the brain" report was a parser bug: the harness missed
  `mcp_tool_call` events (fact:ca3560c736bbd1a41cda1e19).
- Arms that instruct the agent to call a tool fail adherence; harness delivery
  isolates the effect of memory content (Phase 0B pilot memo,
  `benchmarks/agent-brain/temporal-memory/`).
- A 26-task benchmark exists with a prespecified 13-task memory-sensitive
  stratum; recall@5 was 11/26, MRR 0.277 (fact:02dd1672383128a94ffcee37).
  Decision on record: do not rebuild or expand the task set before retrieval
  is validated (fact:8dd50b5e5e499833693bff47).
- Strip committed `.entire/` and `.codex/` side channels uniformly across all
  benchmark arms (fact:6b4add8c4948386e0142bec7).
- Actionability matters: file-only hints were insufficient; exact repair
  guidance plus one regression test produced a focused successful run
  (fact:8cfb111d5ed197a7d4b3e23a).
- Pre-agent test injection was rejected; materialize validation tests after
  the agent runs (fact:0baeb610b017043493b8989d).
- A confirmatory preregistration, power analysis, and a recorded no-go exist
  in `benchmarks/agent-brain/confirmatory/`.

## Phase 1 — Baseline measurement (observational, cheap)

Build a transcript scorer that reads captured Entire sessions from real local
work. No new agent runs are needed.

Per-session metrics:

- Preflight rate: `brain version` + `capabilities` before the first
  substantive step.
- Brief-first rate: `brain brief` before the first Read/Grep on a
  substantive task.
- Recall-before-replace rate: `recall` before proposing to replace an
  existing approach.
- Remember rate: `remember` in sessions that established a durable decision.
- Memory use rate: when brief or recall returned facts, did the agent cite a
  fact id or act on its content later in the session.

Scorer requirements:

- Parse both Bash-invoked CLI calls and `mcp_tool_call` events (the known
  parser-bug class).
- Segment by harness (claude-code, codex) and by task type.

Hand-label a sample (~50 sessions) for retrieval usefulness: precision@k of
returned facts, and an "acted-on" rate per fact.

Output: a baseline report plus a ranked list of the rules agents break most.

## Phase 2 — Controlled A/B on instruction variants

- Reuse the archived 26-task suite and the 13-task memory-sensitive stratum.
  Panel configs exist in `benchmarks/agent-brain/panels/`. Do not build new
  tasks first.
- Arms differ only in instruction wording. Delivery stays constant. Use
  benchmark-neutral capability wording where fairness requires it.
- Two separate designs, because they answer different questions:
  - Adherence arms: instruction wording varies; measure tool-call rates and
    ordering.
  - Usefulness arms: harness-delivered memories (per Phase 0B); measure task
    outcome deltas from memory content and format.
- Metrics: per-rule adherence, task pass rate, tokens, turns, memory-citation
  precision. Paired comparisons. Use the archived power analysis to size runs.

## Phase 3 — Improvement hypotheses to test (ranked)

1. Recall output actionability: include anchor snippets and "how to apply"
   guidance with each fact, not bare fact text.
2. Brief memories-sample framing: test whether agents still stop at the
   sample instead of running targeted recall (issue #335 follow-up).
3. Guide length and structure: a shorter, rule-ranked guide vs the current
   dense one. Keep directive wording; never reintroduce self-assessed exits.
4. Fact text quality at distillation: enforce decision + rationale +
   application phrasing in the distill template.
5. Delivery placement: hook-injected reminders (UserPromptSubmit /
   PreToolUse) vs static guide text.

## Guardrails

- Do not soften the shipped directive constants. `TestNormalGuideStaysDirective`
  pins them, and the 2026-09-14 regression is the reason.
- `guide.go` is mirrored byte-identical with entire-graph. Any guide change
  lands in both repos.
- `benchmarks/agent-brain/` is a sealed archive with integrity tests. New
  eval work goes in a new directory. Never edit archived records.
- Plan artifacts stay in `.context` and Linear. No committed docs.

## Open questions (for Evis)

1. Phase order: start with observational baselining of real sessions, or go
   straight to controlled A/B runs?
2. Which harnesses count: claude-code only, or codex too?
3. Budget: are paid A/B runs pre-approved, or do you want a cost estimate
   gate before Phase 2?
4. Scope: Brain memory instructions only, or the Graph half of the shared
   guide too?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate adherence rows into a baseline report. Python 3.9."""
import json, sys, collections

rows = {}
for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    for line in open(path):
        r = json.loads(line)
        sid = r["session_id"] or r["file"]
        prev = rows.get(sid)
        if prev is None or r["n_lines"] > prev["n_lines"]:
            rows[sid] = r

rows = list(rows.values())


def month(r):
    ts = r.get("first_ts") or ""
    return ts[:7] if ts else "unknown"


def is_substantive(r):
    return r["n_tool_calls"] >= 5 and r["n_user_prompts"] >= 1


def pct(n, d):
    return "%d/%d (%.0f%%)" % (n, d, 100.0 * n / d) if d else "0/0"


subst = [r for r in rows if is_substantive(r)]
codex = [r for r in rows if r["format"] == "codex"]

print("sessions total=%d substantive=%d codex-format=%d" % (len(rows), len(subst), len(codex)))

buckets = collections.defaultdict(list)
for r in subst:
    buckets[month(r)].append(r)

hdr = ("month", "n", "brief", "brief1st", "recall", "remember", "graph", "preflight", "factret", "factcited")
print("\t".join(hdr))
for m in sorted(buckets):
    rs = buckets[m]
    n = len(rs)
    brief = sum(1 for r in rs if r["brief_ran"])
    # brief-first: brief ran and before first exploration (or no exploration)
    b1 = sum(
        1
        for r in rs
        if r["brief_ran"]
        and (
            r["first_explore_idx"] is None
            or (r["first_brief_idx"] is not None and r["first_brief_idx"] <= r["first_explore_idx"])
        )
    )
    recall = sum(1 for r in rs if r["recall_ran"])
    remem = sum(1 for r in rs if r["remember_ran"])
    graph = sum(1 for r in rs if r["graph_cmds"])
    pre = sum(1 for r in rs if r["version_before_brain"] and r["caps_before_brain"])
    factret = sum(1 for r in rs if r["fact_ids_returned"])
    factcit = sum(1 for r in rs if r["fact_ids_cited_later"])
    print("%s\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d" % (m, n, brief, b1, recall, remem, graph, pre, factret, factcit))

n = len(subst)

I'm setting up Phase 2, the controlled A/B harness, while the labelers finish. For the workspaces I'm weighing git worktrees of the repo at a fixed commit against isolated clones, since the runs will edit files and worktrees share one .git directory.

I'm weighing the arm-swap mechanics: editing the guide file in each worktree, uncommitted, so CLAUDE.md's include delivers the arm's instructions. I'm noting the confounds that stay constant across arms, the global CLAUDE.md and the Entire hook, and that the shared brain store only contaminates lightly since each run gets its own branch. I'm also leaning toward a cheaper model for consistency and affordability, while flagging that it won't match production exactly.

I'm settling on the stream-json capture and permission flags for headless runs, then moving on to the four arms: the current guide as shipped, a compact directive with the same core mandates, a neutral capability description, and a no-guide control.

I'm laying out the remaining tasks for the harness: six self-contained ones across a few classes, judged on whether the arms follow the guide rather than on whether the task gets finished. I'm checking that the symbols I'd use, like the agentsetup writer, actually exist before I commit to them.

I'm working through the remaining harness tasks: a history question on the removed semantic retrieval, plus a refactor-scoping task on the facts manifest lock. I'm planning to run 4 arms across 5 tasks with 2 repetitions each, which comes to 40 runs.

I'm planning a usefulness arm for the history tasks, comparing normal recall use against recalled facts injected into the prompt and the brain disabled, to see whether recorded memory improves answers and whether retrieval or injection makes a difference.

I'm adding a couple more why-questions that have recorded ground truth, then checking the symbols and past facts before building anything. I'll run one pilot headless to confirm the stream-json output parses. I'm also checking whether repo hooks such as the SessionStart one could interfere with headless runs; they should be the same across arms. Each run goes in its own worktree under a unique branch so nothing shares stash or refs, and the worktrees get pruned afterward.

I'm writing the arm guide files under the eval directory, with the current arm taken from the repo's shipped guide. Compact and capability get authored by me now, and the global CLAUDE.md's constant instructions stay in place for all arms. I also want to pin the model with `--model` so headless runs don't silently pick up the user's default.
I'm building a headless A/B harness comparing four guide variants across five tasks with two reps each, and running a pilot first to confirm capture works.

Confirmed that `agentsetup.Install` is a real exported symbol and that the trail #278 semantic removal is genuine ground truth. Next I'll set up the guide variants and the runner, starting by pulling the full current agent-guide.md from `.entire/`, which I already have from the system prompt.

I'm drafting the compact guide directive now, with its rules for brain briefs, recall, graph queries, and impact checks before edits. I'll note the "neutral" and "no repository agent guide" arms alongside it so the setup is complete.

The next part is the compact guide directive's rules and the start of the capability-only variant, which describes the brain and graph CLI tools.

I'm now drafting the compact guide directive, plus a capability-only version that just describes the brain and graph CLI tools without prescribing when to use them, and I'm checking whether my current rewritten thinking already covers the tasks I plan to test against.

Next I'm drafting the test tasks: a history question on why the guide uses directive wording, a relationship question about everywhere `Install` is used, a small edit to add a `--branch main` hint, a scope-only refactor of the facts manifest lock, and a history question on whether brain supports semantic retrieval. I still need to check the ground truth for the `Install` callers, and for the regression and wording history behind the first task.

Next I'm checking the write-lock path: the global brain lock scales with total facts, and the manifest update happens under it. I also want a bit more on the trail #278 decision, since the semantic retrieval task depends on it. Then I'll set the runs to 2 reps across the four arms and five tasks, with parallelism 6 in a detached worktree per run.

Next I'm writing the runner script: each run gets a detached git worktree, and the Claude CLI invocation uses headless stream-json output. I'm weighing whether to use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, and I'm considering the risk of running arbitrary commands on the user's machine given the benign tasks.

I'm weighing the remaining concerns about the runner: the headless sessions will pick up the same plugins and hooks in every arm, so that stays constant. Since CLAUDE.md in the worktree loads the swapped guide file, the arm assignment should carry through to each run, and I'm checking whether the entire hooks capturing session data cause any problem.

I'm setting up a small pilot to check the plumbing: one cheap run, the current guide arm, on the first history task. I'm also adding a set of eight extra runs that test the history tasks with memory facts injected into the prompt versus no guide at all. Correctness will be checked by grepping for the expected markers and reading the final answers myself.

# Entire repository agent guide — Graph and Brain

Mandatory rules, in priority order. They apply to every substantive task,
including small edits, follow-ups, specs, and reviews.

1. START every substantive task with:
       entire brain brief "<task>" --json
   Run it before any source reading or searching. Familiarity with the repo
   does not waive this.

2. HISTORY questions (why something was done, what was decided, what was
   tried before) MUST be answered with:
       entire brain recall "<question>" --json
   Never answer history from recollection or source comments. Memories are
   stored per branch; an empty result on a feature branch is not proof of
   absence. Cite fact ids for historical claims.

3. RELATIONSHIP questions (callers, callees, dependents, implementors,
   blast radius) MUST be answered with Graph, even when you know the file:
       entire graph query --repo . --profile full --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "<task>"
   Use `neighbors` for one relationship, `impact` for blast radius.
   Grep may supplement Graph; it never replaces it.

4. BEFORE editing any exported or shared-library symbol, run
   `entire graph impact` on it. Scoping a refactor, writing a spec, and
   reviewing a change count as editing.

5. BEFORE finishing, if you established something durable the code does not
   state (a decision and rationale, an invariant, a gotcha), record it:

#!/bin/zsh
# Run one A/B cell: arm, task, rep. Creates a throwaway worktree on its own
# branch, swaps the agent guide, runs headless claude, stores stream-json.
# Usage: run_ab.sh <arm> <taskid> <rep>
set -u
ARM=$1; TASK_ID=$2; REP=$3
ROOT=/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/denver
EVAL=$ROOT/.context/eval
RUN="ab-${ARM}-${TASK_ID}-r${REP}"
WT=/tmp/brain-ab/$RUN
OUT=$EVAL/runs/$RUN.jsonl
mkdir -p $EVAL/runs /tmp/brain-ab
[ -f "$OUT" ] && [ -s "$OUT" ] && { echo "skip $RUN (exists)"; exit 0; }

source $EVAL/tasks.sh
eval "TASK=\${TASK_${TASK_ID}}"

git -C $ROOT worktree remove --force $WT 2>/dev/null
git -C $ROOT branch -D eval/$RUN 2>/dev/null
git -C $ROOT worktree add -b eval/$RUN $WT HEAD >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "worktree fail $RUN"; exit 1; }
cp $EVAL/arms/$ARM.md $WT/.entire/agent-guide.md

cd $WT && claude -p "$TASK" \
  --model claude-sonnet-5-5 \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --permission-mode bypassPermissions \
  --max-turns 60 \
  > $OUT 2> $EVAL/runs/$RUN.err
rc=$?
cd /
git -C $ROOT worktree remove --force $WT 2>/dev/null
git -C $ROOT branch -D eval/$RUN 2>/dev/null
echo "done $RUN rc=$rc lines=$(wc -l < $OUT)"

# Brain agent-instruction adherence and memory-usefulness analysis

Date: 2026-11-06. Author: Claude (session for Evis). Status: Phase 1 complete,
Phase 2 running.

Artifacts: `.context/eval/` — scorer (`score.py`), aggregates (`aggregate.py`,
`segment.py`), friction counts (`friction.py`), digests (`digests/`), A/B
harness (`run_ab.sh`, `driver.sh`, `run_inject.sh`, `arms/`, `tasks.sh`),
run scorer (`score_runs.py`).

## Corpus

- 319 transcripts from `refs/entire/checkpoints/**` (team-wide, deduped to 56
  sessions) + 138 local Claude Code sessions in entire-brain / entire-graph
  workspaces. After dedup: 149 sessions, 104 substantive (>=5 tool calls).
- 31 Codex sessions touching entire-brain (crude string scoring).
- Window: 2026-10 .. 2026-11 (older local transcripts no longer on disk).

## Phase 1 — observational baseline (Claude Code, substantive sessions, n=104)

| Rule | Rate |
|---|---|
| `brain brief` ran | 80% (83/104) |
| brief BEFORE first exploration | 56% (58/104) |
| `recall` ran | 67% |
| `remember` ran | 62% |
| graph used | 66% |
| preflight `version`+`capabilities` | 0% (capabilities: 2 calls in entire corpus vs 113 `version`) |

Non-meta segment (ordinary coding, not brain-feature work, n=75): brief 76%,
brief-first 56%, recall 63%, remember 57%, graph 60%. The directive guide DOES
trigger tool use; ordering and preflight are the weak rules.

Tool volume: explore=3,618 vs brain=1,036 + graph=305 (27% share) — a different
world from the 0.34% graph share recorded before the directive rewrite.

### Memory usefulness (47 fact-returning sessions, hand-labeled digests)

- Relevance: 79% of sessions had at least one clearly on-task memory; 21%
  tangential only; 0% fully irrelevant. (Conditioned on facts returned at all:
  only 45% of substantive sessions ever saw a fact.)
- Visible use: 38% behavior visibly changed (USED=2), 30% acknowledged only,
  32% ignored returned facts entirely.
- Fact-id citation: 8/381 returned fact ids ever cited again (2%); 4/47
  sessions cited any. Citation is NOT a usable proxy for use.
- Inflation caveat: several "on-task" facts were authored by the same session
  (self-recall), and some came back for unrelated queries (BM25 lexical match).

### Friction (corpus-wide counts)

| Signal | Count |
|---|---|
| recall calls | 1,626 |
| recall returned empty facts | 263 (16%) |
| recall already invoked with `--branch` workaround | 865 (53%) |
| sessions: empty recall then `--branch` retry | 126 |
| sessions: empty recall, NO retry (memories lost) | 87 (41% of empty-hitters) |
| recall/brief piped through `head -c` (truncation risk) | 455 / 320 |
| `brain_locked` errors in results | 75 |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Summarize A/B run rows by arm."""
import json, collections

rows = json.load(open("run_rows.json"))
ab = [r for r in rows if r["run"].startswith("ab-")]
use = [r for r in rows if r["run"].startswith("use-")]

by_arm = collections.defaultdict(list)
for r in ab:
    by_arm[r["arm"]].append(r)


def rate(rs, f):
    n = len(rs)
    k = sum(1 for r in rs if f(r))
    return "%d/%d" % (k, n)


print("arm\tn\tbrief\tbrief1st\trecall\trec-branch\tgraph\timpact\tremember\tmed_turns\tmed_cost\tok_hist(T1,T5)\tok_rel(T2)\tok_scope(T4)")
for arm in ("current", "compact", "capability", "none"):
    rs = by_arm.get(arm, [])
    if not rs:
        continue
    hist = [r for r in rs if r["task"] in ("T1", "T5")]
    rel = [r for r in rs if r["task"] == "T2"]
    scope = [r for r in rs if r["task"] == "T4"]
    turns = sorted(r["turns"] or 0 for r in rs)
    costs = sorted(r["cost"] or 0 for r in rs)
    print("\t".join([
        arm, str(len(rs)),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["brief"] > 0),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["brief_first"]),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["recall"] > 0),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["recall_branch"] > 0),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["graph_q"] > 0),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["impact"] > 0),
        rate(rs, lambda r: r["remember"] > 0),
        str(turns[len(turns) // 2] if turns else "-"),
        "%.2f" % costs[len(costs) // 2] if costs else "-",
        rate(hist, lambda r: r["ok"]),
        rate(rel, lambda r: r["ok"]),
        rate(scope, lambda r: r["ok"]),
    ]))

print()
print("usefulness runs (tasks T1/T5):")
print("mode\tn\tok\tmed_turns\tmed_cost")
by_mode = collections.defaultdict(list)
for r in use:
    by_mode[r["arm"]].append(r)  # arm field holds mode for use- runs
for mode, rs in sorted(by_mode.items()):
    turns = sorted(r["turns"] or 0 for r in rs)
    costs = sorted(r["cost"] or 0 for r in rs)
    print("%s\t%d\t%s\t%s\t%.2f" % (mode, len(rs), rate(rs, lambda r: r["ok"]), turns[len(turns) // 2] if turns else "-", costs[len(costs) // 2] if costs else 0))
# per-task detail for ok
print()
print("per-task ok detail:")
for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r["task"], r["arm"], r["rep"])):
    if r["task"] in ("T1", "T2", "T4", "T5"):
        print("%s ok=%s brief=%d recall=%d(+%d branch) graph=%d impact=%d turns=%s cost=%s" % (
            r["run"], r["ok"], r["brief"], r["recall"], r["recall_branch"], r["graph_q"], r["impact"], r["turns"], r["cost"]))

  mostly read-only), but even the scoping/fix tasks never triggered it.

leaks into commits, code comments, and docs — no-brain arms answered history
questions via git archaeology, honestly (no hallucinated history observed;
the none-arm scoping run explicitly said it found no prior design notes).

- Efficiency: history tasks (T1/T5) median turns — current 7, compact 8.5,
  capability/none 11.5; inject 8 (T5: 4–5), floor 12. Memory access cuts
  turns ~30–40%.
- Scoping task (T4) cost: none $1.59/$2.27 vs compact $1.03/$1.13 and
  current $1.42/$1.59 — Brain+Graph roughly halves the cost of scoping.

  contention measurements, rejected approaches); none arms missed them.

  facts outperform agent-driven retrieval, consistent with the Phase 0B
  recorded finding that harness delivery beats instructed tool calls.

the production incident record and the observational baseline.

   and both recall templates: memories are per-branch; an empty recall on a
   feature branch MUST be retried with `--branch main` (and say so in the
   answer). Today 41% of sessions that hit an empty recall never retry and
   silently lose available memories; `recall --branch` is recorded as
   "exists but is undocumented" (fact:d88c9ece).
2. Fix the dead preflight rule: `capabilities` ran twice in the entire corpus
   (vs 113 `version`). A mandate nobody follows erodes the guide's authority.
   Either drop capabilities from the preflight or fold it into one command.
3. Adopt the compact directive guide (~40 lines, `.context/eval/arms/compact.md`
   is the tested draft): equal adherence, better ordering, cheaper. Never ship
   capability-only wording.
4. Prescribe a bounded-output idiom: agents invented `head -c` (455 recalls,
   320 briefs) and it cuts JSON mid-payload — on main the brief's facts run
   ~34KB before history. Tell agents to use `-n`/`--limit` and never `head -c`.

   of Claude Code's on the same guide (brief 52% vs 80%).

   note in the payload). Dedupe rows (one observed recall: 74% duplicates).
   Cap payload size so truncation is never needed.
7. brief: enforce a size budget (compact_brief_formats exists but is unused);
   on feature branches include mainline facts; drop/trim facts_pending_review;
   put warnings before 34KB of content, not after.

   38% of fact-returning sessions visibly used them; recorded evidence

   recurring warnings train agents to ignore the payload and send them on
   side quests.

    the existing UserPromptSubmit hook instead of relying on the agent to
    fetch them. Inject arm: 4/4 correct at ~half the turns; floor 2/4. This
    also matches the recorded Phase 0B causal-delivery finding.

# Brain agent-instruction adherence and memory-usefulness analysis

Date: 2026-11-06. Author: Claude (session for Evis). Status: Phase 1 complete,
Phase 2 running.

Artifacts: `.context/eval/` — scorer (`score.py`), aggregates (`aggregate.py`,
`segment.py`), friction counts (`friction.py`), digests (`digests/`), A/B
harness (`run_ab.sh`, `driver.sh`, `run_inject.sh`, `arms/`, `tasks.sh`),
run scorer (`score_runs.py`).

## Corpus

- 319 transcripts from `refs/entire/checkpoints/**` (team-wide, deduped to 56
  sessions) + 138 local Claude Code sessions in entire-brain / entire-graph
  workspaces. After dedup: 149 sessions, 104 substantive (>=5 tool calls).
- 31 Codex sessions touching entire-brain (crude string scoring).
- Window: 2026-10 .. 2026-11 (older local transcripts no longer on disk).

## Phase 1 — observational baseline (Claude Code, substantive sessions, n=104)

| Rule | Rate |
|---|---|
| `brain brief` ran | 80% (83/104) |
| brief BEFORE first exploration | 56% (58/104) |
| `recall` ran | 67% |
| `remember` ran | 62% |
| graph used | 66% |
| preflight `version`+`capabilities` | 0% (capabilities: 2 calls in entire corpus vs 113 `version`) |

Non-meta segment (ordinary coding, not brain-feature work, n=75): brief 76%,
brief-first 56%, recall 63%, remember 57%, graph 60%. The directive guide DOES
trigger tool use; ordering and preflight are the weak rules.

Tool volume: explore=3,618 vs brain=1,036 + graph=305 (27% share) — a different
world from the 0.34% graph share recorded before the directive rewrite.

### Memory usefulness (47 fact-returning sessions, hand-labeled digests)

- Relevance: 79% of sessions had at least one clearly on-task memory; 21%
  tangential only; 0% fully irrelevant. (Conditioned on facts returned at all:
  only 45% of substantive sessions ever saw a fact.)
- Visible use: 38% behavior visibly changed (USED=2), 30% acknowledged only,
  32% ignored returned facts entirely.
- Fact-id citation: 8/381 returned fact ids ever cited again (2%); 4/47
  sessions cited any. Citation is NOT a usable proxy for use.
- Inflation caveat: several "on-task" facts were authored by the same session
  (self-recall), and some came back for unrelated queries (BM25 lexical match).

### Friction (corpus-wide counts)

| Signal | Count |
|---|---|
| recall calls | 1,626 |
| recall returned empty facts | 263 (16%) |
| recall already invoked with `--branch` workaround | 865 (53%) |
| sessions: empty recall then `--branch` retry | 126 |
| sessions: empty recall, NO retry (memories lost) | 87 (41% of empty-hitters) |
| recall/brief piped through `head -c` (truncation risk) | 455 / 320 |
| `brain_locked` errors in results | 75 |
| manifest-mismatch warnings in results | 440 |
| duplicate-fact warnings | 68 |
| hardlinked-history-index errors | 48 |

Labeler-observed failure modes, recurring:
1. Per-branch recall scoping dominates: fresh feature branches return
   `facts: []`/`null`; agents must know to retry `--branch main`; many don't.
2. Agents mis-parse recall JSON (read `memories`/`results`/`content` keys
   instead of `facts`) and silently drop returned facts.
3. Brief history excerpts are often machine noise (raw tool_end JSON records,
   command lines), not conversational content.
4. Duplicate facts (one recall: 74% duplicate rows) and "pending fact review"
   walls flood output.
5. Warnings (manifest behind, stale semantic index) send agents on side quests.

### Codex (n=29 substantive)

brief 52%, recall 41%, remember 45%, graph 45% — far below Claude Code on the
same guide. The codex-skill templates deserve their own pass.

## Phase 2 — controlled A/B (results pending)

Grid: arms {current, compact, capability, none} x tasks {T1 history, T2
relationship, T3 small fix, T4 refactor scope, T5 history+rec} x 2 reps,
claude -p, sonnet, fresh worktree per run, guide file swapped per arm.
Usefulness: tasks T1/T5 with {inject (facts in prompt, no guide), floor (no
guide)} x 2 reps vs the tools arm from the grid.

## Phase 2 — controlled A/B (48 paid runs, sonnet, headless)

Grid: arms {current 178-line guide, compact 40-line directive, capability-only,
none} x tasks {T1 history-why, T2 relationship, T3 small fix, T4 refactor
scope, T5 history+recommendation} x 2 reps. Fresh worktree per run, guide file
swapped per arm. Usefulness: T1/T5 with {inject: top recall facts in the
